newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Arnotts hit by extortion threat.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Arnotts hit by extortion threat.

text.p: Retailers in New South Wales and Queensland states removed thousands of packets of Arnotts Ltd biscuits from their shelves on Friday after an extortionist threatened to plant poisoned biscuits in stores from next Monday.
Arnotts ordered the recall, saying the safety and welfare of its customers was paramount, although it believed all Arnotts products on supermarket shelves and now in homes were safe.
"Clearly that decision was not taken lightly and, by God, I wish I didn't have to take it," Arnotts chief executive Chris Roberts told a news conference in Brisbane.
Arnotts is about 70 percent owned by Campbell Soup Co of the United States.
Queensland police revealed late on Thursday that an extortionist had threatened to plant poisoned biscuits in supermarkets unless police involved in a 1991 murder case underwent a lie detector test.

The extortionist laced Monte Carlo cream biscuits made by Arnotts with a pesticide and sent packages of the poisoned biscuits, along with a letter, to Arnotts, politicians and a media organisation on February 3, police said.
The letter demanded that New South Wales police involved in the murder investigation of bookmaker Peter Wade and his girlfriend in 1991 undergo a polygraph test by February 17.
The letter claimed Ronald Thomas, 46, who is serving a life sentence for the shooting murders was innocent and that the real killers remained free.
The Australian Supermarket Institute said on Friday that major retailing chains were removing the entire Arnotts range from sale in Queensland and New South Wales at the request of Arnotts.
The institute's members include Woolworths Ltd, Coles Myer Ltd, Franklins, Davids Ltd and Foodland Associated Ltd.
Roberts said the evidence showed clearly that the threat only related to products in the two states, and exports to New Zealand and Asia would not be affected.
The recall would have a cost to Arnotts, with the value of the stock removed running into millions of dollars, he said.
"The extent of that cost will be determined by the period that our products will be off the shelves in New South Wales and Queensland," he said.
Production at Arnotts factories would continue and no staff would be laid off in the foreseeable future.
Food analysts said the withdrawal would have a short-term impact on Arnotts' earnings, but the long-term impact was less certain.
"It all depends on the length of time and that sort of thing. It could just be devastating," said one.
However, another said the share price of the tightly held stock should not be affected too greatly.
"In the short-term earnings would be affected but the share price is not necessarily about short-term earnings," he said.
Detective superintendent Ron Pickering, who heads the investigation, said Arnotts was an innocent victim in the extortion threat, and warned other food companies could become involved.
"It is not only Arnotts that we would be concerned about," he said, adding that the poisoned biscuits were not laced in the production process, but after being bought by the extortionist.
Pickering said shoppers should examine the packaging of food they purchased, especially cream biscuits, in case it had been tampered with.
Arnotts asked for trading in its shares to be suspended prior to the start of trade on Friday.
Arnotts' shares closed up five cents at A$8.75 on Thursday.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
